source_text: Oportuerat quidem apud humanum genus reverentiam omnium.vigere virtutum; oportuerat resisti sapienti semper mente criminibus et demereri bonis studiis Conditoris favorem; dignum erat postremo, ut quia hic continuae devotionis prior et felicior gradus cum rarus tum arduus etiam nimis videtur, vel diu fota vitia respui et ad emendationis ac paenitentiae praesidium rediri. Oportuerat certe vel in hoc inviolabilem Dei manere reverentiam, ut non nobis esset necesse divinam legem tanto vindicare certamine, verum, quia eo usque peccantium furore perventum est, ut summis laboribus Deum iustum esse doceamus, ipsius iustitiae, cuius causa agitur, praesumentes auxilium, quae libro promisimus praecedente, reddamus.
pass_a_gloss: It had indeed been fitting that reverence of all virtues should flourish among the human race; it had been fitting that crimes always be resisted with a wise mind and that the Creator's favor be earned by good studies; lastly it was worthy that, because this prior and happier step of continual devotion seems both rare and even excessively hard, even vices long cherished be spat out and a return be made to the shelter of correction and repentance. It had certainly been fitting that reverence of God remain inviolable at least in this, that it not be necessary for us to vindicate the divine law by so great a contest; but because it has been reached by the frenzy of those sinning to the point that we teach with utmost labors that God is just, presuming upon the help of the very justice whose cause is being pleaded, let us render what we promised in the preceding book.

lemmas.lexica: LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: Respect for every virtue ought to flourish among the human race. People ought always to resist wrongdoing with a wise mind and win their Creator’s favor by good pursuits. Or at least, since this first and happier level of constant devotion seems both rare and exceedingly difficult, they ought to reject even long-cherished vices and return to the shelter of reform and repentance. Surely reverence for God ought at least to have remained untouched in this respect: we should not have to defend the divine law in so great a struggle. But the frenzy of sinners has reached the point where we must labor strenuously to teach that God is just. So, trusting in the help of the very justice whose cause we plead, let us now fulfill what we promised in the preceding book.

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: Julian means Scripture's legal/authoritative witness, especially the divine Law as teacher of justice.
rejected: natural law (unless the sentence is philosophical)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
